questions.stem: Which set of features is shared by all viruses?

options.text: A nucleic-acid genome, a protein capsid, no cytoplasm, and few or no enzymes
options.why: These are the shared features in the syllabus. The genome can be DNA or RNA, while the capsid is made of protein.

options.text: A DNA genome, a protein capsid, ribosomes, and enzymes for independent metabolism
options.why: Some viral genomes are RNA, and viruses lack ribosomes and independent metabolism. Those cellular features would remove their dependence on a host.

options.text: An RNA genome, a lipid envelope, cytoplasm, and enzymes for protein synthesis
options.why: DNA viruses exist, and many viruses have no envelope. Viruses also lack cytoplasm and don't carry out their own protein synthesis.

options.text: A nucleic-acid genome, a cell membrane, cytoplasm, and a small number of ribosomes
options.why: That describes a reduced cell more closely than a virus. A viral capsid is universal, but cytoplasm and ribosomes are absent.

questions.stem: Why must viruses use host cells to produce new virions?

options.text: They lack ribosomes and sufficient metabolic machinery for independent protein synthesis and reproduction
options.why: The host supplies ribosomes, energy, materials and other machinery. Viral genes redirect those resources toward making viral components.

options.text: Their capsids prevent nucleic acids from being copied until a host digests the protein coat
options.why: A capsid protects the genome during transmission. Host dependence comes from missing cellular machinery, not from the capsid blocking replication.

options.text: Their genomes contain no genes and therefore provide no instructions for making viral proteins
options.why: Viral genomes do contain genes for viral proteins and replication functions. The missing part is the complete machinery needed to express and copy them independently.

options.text: They obtain all genetic information from the host chromosome during every infection cycle
options.why: A virus brings its own genetic information into the infection. It uses host resources, but it doesn't obtain its entire genome from the host.

questions.stem: Which comparison of bacteriophage lambda, coronaviruses and HIV is accurate?

options.text: Lambda has double-stranded DNA, while coronaviruses and HIV have single-stranded RNA
options.why: Lambda is a DNA bacteriophage. Coronaviruses are positive-sense RNA viruses, while HIV is an RNA retrovirus.

options.text: Lambda and HIV lack envelopes, while coronaviruses obtain envelopes from host cells
options.why: Lambda lacks an envelope, but HIV and coronaviruses are both enveloped. Their envelopes contain viral proteins.

options.text: Coronaviruses contain reverse transcriptase, while HIV translates its RNA genome directly
options.why: Reverse transcriptase belongs to HIV. Coronaviral positive-sense RNA can function as mRNA after entering a host cell.

options.text: All three contain double-stranded DNA protected by differently shaped protein capsids
options.why: Only lambda has a double-stranded DNA genome. Coronaviruses and HIV carry single-stranded RNA.

questions.stem: What must happen before a negative-sense RNA viral genome can be translated?

options.text: It must be copied into complementary positive-sense mRNA
options.why: Ribosomes translate positive-sense mRNA. An RNA-dependent RNA polymerase must make that positive-sense copy first.

options.text: It must be integrated directly into the host chromosome
options.why: Integration is part of the retroviral route and lysogeny in temperate phages. Negative-sense RNA instead needs a positive-sense RNA copy.

options.text: It must be converted into protein by reverse transcriptase
options.why: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA; it doesn't make protein. Ribosomes carry out translation.

options.text: It must be joined to a capsid protein that acts as a ribosome
options.why: Capsid proteins protect the genome and don't act as ribosomes. Viral proteins are translated by host ribosomes.

questions.stem: Which event occurs at the start of bacteriophage lambda’s lytic cycle?

options.text: The phage attaches to a receptor and injects its DNA
options.why: The phage recognizes the bacterium through attachment proteins. Its DNA enters while the head and tail remain outside.

options.text: The entire phage enters the bacterial cytoplasm by endocytosis
options.why: Bacteria don't take lambda in by endocytosis. Lambda remains outside and injects its DNA through the bacterial surface.

options.text: The bacterial chromosome enters the phage capsid for replication
options.why: The direction is backwards. Phage DNA enters the bacterium and uses host resources to replicate.

options.text: The phage divides by binary fission beside the bacterial chromosome
options.why: Binary fission is cell division. Viral parts are produced separately inside the host and assembled into virions.

questions.stem: What happens to lambda DNA during the lysogenic cycle?

options.text: It integrates into the bacterial chromosome as a prophage
options.why: The prophage is copied whenever the host chromosome replicates and can pass to daughter cells without immediate lysis.

options.text: It is translated into capsid protein before any DNA replication
options.why: DNA isn't translated directly. It must be transcribed into mRNA, and immediate capsid production belongs to lytic replication.

options.text: It remains inside the external capsid while the bacterium divides
options.why: The viral DNA has been injected into the bacterium. During lysogeny it sits in the host chromosome, not in an external capsid.

options.text: It destroys the bacterial chromosome and immediately directs host-cell lysis
options.why: That describes destructive lytic infection. During lysogeny, the host chromosome survives and carries the prophage.

questions.stem: A bacterial lineage carries lambda DNA for many generations without producing virions. Which event could later begin virion production?

options.text: Induction causing the prophage to leave the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle
options.why: A trigger such as DNA damage can cause prophage excision. Viral replication, assembly and lysis can then follow.

options.text: Conjugation causing the prophage to become a bacterial plasmid and divide independently
options.why: Conjugation transfers bacterial DNA between cells. The switch described here is prophage induction into the lytic cycle.

options.text: Binary fission causing the prophage capsid to rupture inside each daughter cell
options.why: A prophage is integrated DNA, not a complete capsid. Binary fission copies it without producing virions.

options.text: Translation causing viral RNA to integrate permanently into the bacterial chromosome
options.why: Translation makes protein from mRNA and doesn't integrate genomes. Lambda’s prophage consists of DNA already integrated in the chromosome.

questions.stem: Which observation best supports the idea that viruses have several origins?

options.text: Viruses differ greatly in genome type, structure and replication mechanism
options.why: Their extreme diversity fits the idea that different viral groups arose through different evolutionary routes.

options.text: Every virus contains the same genes arranged in the same order
options.why: Viruses don't share one universal set of genes in one arrangement. Their genetic systems are highly diverse.

options.text: Every virus has an envelope derived from the same ancestral cell membrane
options.why: Many viruses have no envelope. Enveloped viruses obtain lipid membrane from their current host cells.

options.text: Viruses reproduce independently by one conserved form of binary fission
options.why: Viruses depend on host cells and don't undergo binary fission. Their replication routes vary widely.

questions.stem: What does the progressive hypothesis propose about viral origins?

options.text: Cellular genetic elements gained the ability to move between cells and acquired protective structures
options.why: This is also called the escape hypothesis. Mobile genetic material may have become an infectious system.

options.text: Free-living cells lost structures and functions as they became increasingly dependent on hosts
options.why: That's the regressive or reduction hypothesis. It begins with cellular parasites becoming less complex.

options.text: Viruses existed before cells and later donated every cellular gene to the first organisms
options.why: That isn't the progressive hypothesis. The progressive route begins with genetic elements from existing cells.

options.text: Unrelated viruses independently evolved capsids because they faced similar selection pressures
options.why: That's an explanation based on convergent evolution. It explains similarity, not the progressive origin route itself.

questions.stem: Why can many RNA viruses evolve rapidly?

options.text: Frequent copying errors, large populations and short generation times produce many variants
options.why: Mutation supplies variation quickly, and selection can increase variants favored by immunity, drugs or transmission conditions.

options.text: Host cells deliberately alter viral RNA so the infection can adapt to antiviral drugs
options.why: Mutations don't arise because adaptation is needed. Copying errors create variants, and drugs select among them.

options.text: RNA viruses reproduce by accurate binary fission but exchange genes with bacterial plasmids
options.why: Viruses don't reproduce by binary fission. Rapid change often follows error-prone genome copying and intense selection.

options.text: Every new virion receives genetic material from a different host-cell chromosome
options.why: Virions receive copies of the viral genome, not random host chromosomes. Variation mainly comes from mutation and, in some viruses, recombination or reassortment.

questions.stem: Which process causes antigenic shift in influenza viruses?

options.text: Reassortment of genome segments from different influenza viruses in one host cell
options.why: Influenza has a segmented genome. Mixing segments can create a major new combination of surface antigens.

options.text: Gradual accumulation of mutations in genes encoding viral surface antigens
options.why: That's antigenic drift. It produces smaller changes that accumulate over time.

options.text: Integration of the influenza genome into a bacterial chromosome as a prophage
options.why: That describes lysogeny in a bacteriophage such as lambda. Influenza infects animal cells and doesn't form a bacterial prophage.

options.text: Reverse transcription of influenza RNA into DNA followed by chromosome integration
options.why: That's the retroviral route used by HIV. Influenza is an RNA virus but not a retrovirus.

questions.stem: Why is a combination of antiretroviral drugs used to treat HIV?

options.text: Resistance to several drugs with different targets requires a less probable combination of mutations
options.why: A variant resistant to one drug may still be stopped by the others. This reduces the chance that resistant HIV will reproduce.

options.text: Each drug increases HIV’s mutation rate until the viral genome becomes unable to function
options.why: Treatment isn't intended to drive harmful mutation. The drugs inhibit different stages of viral replication.

options.text: Different drugs provide the ribosomes and enzymes that HIV lacks outside a host cell
options.why: Host cells provide the machinery HIV uses. Antiretroviral drugs inhibit viral processes rather than supplying missing structures.

options.text: One drug prevents antigenic drift while the others prevent influenza-style antigenic shift
options.why: Antigenic shift is associated with reassortment in segmented viruses such as influenza. HIV treatment targets its replication cycle.
